lead: The Born-Oppenheimer approximation says electrons move much faster than nuclei, so their motions can be treated separately. The Franck-Condon principle uses that separation: during an electronic absorption, the nuclei hardly move, so the transition is vertical on a potential-energy diagram. The chapter explains potential-energy curves, vibrational levels and the overlap of vibrational wavefunctions, and shows why UV-visible bands have vibrational structure. It is used to read band shapes in UV-visible spectra, to understand colour, and to interpret photochemical excitation before relaxation and reaction steps.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for photon energy, Chapter 2.3 for electronic transitions, and Chapter 2.4 for vibrational levels.

blocks.text: An electron has mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. A proton has mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, about 1836 times larger. In a molecule the nuclei move slowly compared with the electrons. When a photon excites an electron, the electron cloud changes in about 10⁻¹⁵ s, while a bond vibration takes about 10⁻¹³ s. The nuclei hardly move during the electronic jump.

Born and Oppenheimer turned this into a working approximation. Fix the nuclear positions R. Solve the electronic problem for those fixed nuclei. Add the nuclear repulsion to the electronic energy to get the total potential-energy curve U(R) that controls nuclear motion. R is the internuclear distance. The molecular wavefunction, with rotation ignored, is a product: Ψ ≈ ψ_elec(r;R) χ_nuc(R). Here r stands for electron coordinates, ψ_elec is the electronic wavefunction, and χ_nuc is the nuclear vibrational wavefunction. Rotation is not resolved here.

blocks.where: Ψ is the molecular wavefunction with rotation ignored; ψ_elec is the electronic part for fixed nuclei; χ_nuc is the nuclear vibrational part (rotation ignored here); r is the set of electron coordinates; R is the set of internuclear distances.

blocks.text: The electronic energy depends on R only as a parameter. At each R the electrons adjust instantly. The nuclei then move on the single curve U(R). This separation is the Born-Oppenheimer approximation. It fails when two electronic states come very close, but it works well for ordinary UV-visible absorption.

Every electronic state has its own potential-energy curve. The ground-state curve has a minimum at the equilibrium internuclear distance R_e. At shorter R the nuclei repel strongly and U rises. At longer R the curve flattens towards dissociation. The excited-state curve lies higher. Its minimum may sit at a different R_e, because the excited electron changes bonding.

Vibrational levels are quantized inside each curve. For a harmonic model, E_v = (v + ½)hν. v = 0, 1, 2, ... is the vibrational quantum number; ν is the vibrational frequency; h is the Planck constant. The lowest level is v = 0 with zero-point energy ½hν. At room temperature most molecules occupy v = 0. Each level is drawn as a horizontal line inside the well.

items: R_e is the internuclear distance at the minimum of a curve.
A vertical line keeps R fixed; a slanted line would let R change during the jump.
The excited molecule later relaxes to its own minimum, but that happens after absorption.

blocks.text: The Franck-Condon principle says an electronic transition is fast compared with nuclear motion. On a U(R) diagram, draw the transition as a vertical line at fixed R. R does not change during absorption. The electronic state changes; the vibrational wavefunction does not have time to change.

For a given allowed electronic transition, the vibronic intensity is proportional to |μ_el|² |S|². μ_el is the electronic transition dipole moment. S is the overlap integral: S = ∫ χ_v'* χ_v'' dR. χ_v'' is the vibrational wavefunction of the lower electronic state, with quantum number v''. χ_v' is the vibrational wavefunction of the upper state, with v'. The Franck-Condon factor |S|² controls the pattern of vibrational line intensities. A large |S|² gives a strong line. A near-zero |S|² gives a weak line. When μ_el is nearly constant over the relevant R, |S|² alone sets the relative intensities.

Different v' levels give lines at slightly different photon energies. The complete UV-visible band is the envelope of these lines. If the two curves have the same R_e, the 0→0 line is strongest. If the excited curve is shifted, the vertical jump from R_e of the ground state lands where upper-state wavefunctions with v' > 0 have large amplitude. Then the band peaks at 0→2 or 0→3, for example. This is why band shapes carry vibrational information.

figure.caption: Two potential-energy curves against internuclear distance in arbitrary units. The excited curve is 4 energy units above the ground curve and has the same minimum at R = 1.2. An electronic absorption would be a vertical jump at fixed R; only the curves are drawn here.

spec.aria: Two potential-energy curves against internuclear distance in arbitrary units; the excited curve lies above the ground curve and has the same minimum position.

examples.question: A C=O chromophore absorbs ultraviolet light at 280 nm. (a) Find the photon energy in electronvolts. (b) Explain why the electronic transition is drawn vertical on a potential-energy diagram.
steps: Convert wavelength to photon energy with E(eV) = 1240 / λ(nm). The constant 1240 is hc in eV nm.
Put λ = 280 nm: E = 1240 / 280 = 4.4286 eV, which rounds to 4.43 eV.
In joules, E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)(2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)/(280 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 7.10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The eV value is the usual UV-visible unit.
The electronic jump takes about 10⁻¹⁵ s; a C=O vibration takes about 10⁻¹³ s. The nuclei are nearly fixed during absorption.
Draw a vertical line at fixed internuclear distance from the ground curve to the excited curve. The molecule later relaxes to the excited-state minimum, but that is not the absorbing step.
examples.answer: The photon energy is 4.43 eV; the transition is vertical because the nuclei hardly move during the fast electronic jump.

traps: Saying the nuclei move during absorption. In the Franck-Condon picture R is fixed for the jump; nuclear relaxation comes afterwards.
Confusing the vertical transition with the equilibrium geometry of the excited state. The vertical landing point is usually not the excited-state minimum.
Assuming the excited-state curve always has the same R_e as the ground state. A different R_e shifts the strongest vibrational line.
Forgetting that the overlap is between vibrational wavefunctions, not between electronic wavefunctions.
Using E = 1240/λ with λ in metres. The 1240 shortcut needs λ in nanometres to give eV.

quiz.q: State the Born-Oppenheimer approximation in one sentence.
quiz.a: Electrons move much faster than nuclei, so electronic and nuclear motions can be separated and the electrons are treated for fixed nuclear positions.

quiz.q: State the Franck-Condon principle in one sentence.
quiz.a: An electronic transition is so fast that the nuclei do not move during it, so the transition is vertical at fixed internuclear distance.

quiz.q: Why is an electronic transition drawn vertically on a potential-energy diagram?
quiz.a: The electronic jump takes about 10⁻¹⁵ s, while nuclear vibration takes about 10⁻¹³ s. The internuclear distance is nearly unchanged during absorption, so R is held fixed.

quiz.q: What does the overlap integral S measure?
quiz.a: S = ∫ χ_v'* χ_v'' dR measures how much the upper-state vibrational wavefunction overlaps the lower-state vibrational wavefunction. For a given allowed electronic transition, the vibronic intensity is proportional to |μ_el|² |S|², where μ_el is the electronic transition dipole moment. The Franck-Condon factor |S|² controls the pattern of vibrational line intensities.

quiz.q: A chromophore absorbs at 350 nm. Find the photon energy in eV using E = 1240/λ(nm).
Two electronic states have the same R_e. Which vibrational line of the absorption band is expected to be strongest, and why?
quiz.a: The 0→0 line is strongest. The v = 0 vibrational wavefunctions of the two states have maximum overlap when their equilibrium distances coincide, so S is largest for 0→0.

quiz.q: Explain why a shifted excited-state curve gives a broad band with several vibrational peaks.
quiz.a: The vertical jump from the ground-state R_e lands at a different point on the excited curve. Several upper vibrational levels then have significant overlap with the ground v = 0 level. Each overlap gives a line, and their envelope is the broad band.

beyond: Not for the exam. Femtosecond spectroscopy watches nuclear motion after excitation, and the Franck-Condon envelope helps assign those signals. Computational chemistry uses Born-Oppenheimer surfaces to predict UV-visible spectra and photochemical pathways. Search for “Franck-Condon factors”, “vertical excitation energy” and “potential-energy surface” to go further.
